title: The biggest tile for a 48 by 18 floor
hook: Identical square tiles, no cutting. How big can they be? Try sizes, or try scissors.

knows: what a square and a rectangle are
doesNotKnow: that the greatest common divisor survives cutting off squares (gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b))

misconception: Finding the greatest common divisor means testing every smaller number.
objective: The learner can find the largest square tile for a 48 by 18 floor by cutting off the biggest squares (18, 18, 12, 6, 6) and explain why the last square, 6, is the answer.

claims.text: The largest identical square that tiles a 48 by 18 floor exactly is 6 by 6.
claims.source: gcd(48, 18) = 6: 48 = 2 × 18 + 12, 18 = 1 × 12 + 6, 12 = 2 × 6. Builder ran Euclid in Node: 6. 3 also divides both but is smaller; 9 does not divide 48.

claims.text: Cutting the biggest square that fits from 48 by 18, again and again, cuts squares of 18, 18, 12, 6 and 6, and the last strip, 12 by 6, splits into exactly two 6-squares.
claims.source: Demo.tsx cuts(): sides [18, 18, 12, 6, 6]; rectangle after the third cut is 12 × 6. Builder re-ran the loop in Node.

claims.text: A 6-square tiles the whole 48 by 18 floor: 8 across, 3 down, 24 tiles.
Cutting off a square never changes which tiles fit: a tile that fits the floor and the square also fits what is left.
claims.source: If t divides a and b then t divides a − b, and conversely if t divides b and a − b it divides a; so the common divisors of (a, b) and (a − b, b) are the same (Euclid, Elements VII.2; Hardy and Wright, Theorem 4 ff.).

claims.text: The method took 5 cuts here, instead of testing every size up to 18.
claims.source: Demo.tsx CUTS.length = 5. Testing every candidate side from 18 down to 1 is up to 18 tries; 18 here is the shorter side.
Euclid, Elements, Book VII, Propositions 1 and 2 (repeated subtraction to find the greatest common measure); Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 2, 4.5.2.

recall.question: You cut the biggest squares from a 30 by 12 rectangle: 12, 12, then 6, 6. What is the largest square tile for 30 by 12?
recall.why: The last square that fits exactly is 6, and cutting squares never changes which tiles fit, so 6 is the largest common tile (gcd(30, 12) = 6).
